briefing.text: Target population definition: 'SV-driven TXR1 target-mediated activation' is not 'any SV near TXR1' and not 'high TXR1 expression'. Only a minority of SVs change expression of nearby genes. A case should need (a) a mechanistically plausible breakpoint topology (a promoter/enhancer-facing one; the library expects this to be the P2T category in this registry, with INV/D2T or distant junctions likely passengers - verify this against the data and any data dictionary rather than assuming it), and (b) functional evidence that the rearranged haplotype drives expression: allele-specific expression from the SV-carrying haplotype, phase-consistent, plus overexpression. Check: cross-tabulate breakpoint_topology with breakpoint_distance_kb, target_ase_alt_fraction, phase_consistency, phase_linked_reads and txr1_log_tpm. Define target-positive by topology + breakpoint QC + haplotype-consistent ASE (and proximity), state the rule before looking at outcomes, report how many cases each rule admits, and show how the estimates move under alternative rules.
briefing.reason: Every requested number is conditional on who is in the target population; a wrong case definition changes all four outputs.

briefing.text: Breakpoint call quality: long-read SV breakpoints in segmental duplications, low-complexity sequence, low-MAPQ regions, regions with long microhomology, or supported by few split molecules are often false positives. Counting every reported breakpoint as SV-positive misclassifies the target population and dilutes the effect. Check: among cases with breakpoint_topology != NONE, inspect mapq_median, segmental_dup_overlap, low_complexity_score, homology_bp, split_molecule_count relative to molecule_depth, and read_n50. Apply pre-specified QC filters before classifying cases (e.g. minimum supporting molecules scaled to depth, adequate MAPQ, no segmental-duplication overlap) and run a sensitivity analysis with stricter and looser filters.
briefing.reason: Artefactual SV calls would put non-target tumors into the target population and bias the effect and toxicity estimates.

briefing.text: Purity and copy number: raw alt_molecule_fraction and raw ASE fraction depend on tumor purity, local copy number and ploidy/WGD. A low raw fraction in a low-purity sample can still be a clonal event, and a high fraction in an amplified segment can overstate support. Check: compare alt_molecule_fraction with tumor_purity, local_total_copy, tumor_ploidy and wgd_flag, and compute an approximate purity- and copy-adjusted cancer-cell fraction. Use adjusted fractions, not fixed cutoffs on raw fractions, when calling target activation.
briefing.reason: Fixed raw cutoffs would wrongly drop low-purity true positives and admit amplified false positives, changing the target population.

briefing.text: Expression is confounded by lineage and batch: TXR1 expression tracks a lineage program (lineage_marker_log_tpm, lineage_class) and may vary with expression_batch, library size and RNA quality. Defining activation by high TXR1 TPM would select on lineage or batch rather than SV-driven activation. Check: regress txr1_log_tpm on lineage marker, housekeeping expression, batch, purity and rna_quality, and see whether candidate SV-positive cases remain outliers on the residual. Use lineage- and batch-adjusted expression only as supporting evidence for the SV call, never as the definition. Lineage may itself be prognostic, so include lineage_class as a confounder in the effect model.
briefing.reason: Affects both the case definition (expression must not stand in for SV-driven activation) and the confounder set.

briefing.text: Time zero and cohort selection: define the cohort only from information available at time zero. Restrict to analysis_set==1 and confirm that eligibility, therapy_class and covariates are fixed at time_zero_day; tabulate analysis_set against therapy_class and assessed16. Never select cases on post-baseline information: do not filter on assessed16, and keep unassessed cases in the denominator. Selecting on post-time-zero information causes selection or immortal-time bias.
briefing.reason: The task fixes the population 'at time zero'; a cohort built with later information answers a different question.

briefing.text: Confounding by indication and the estimand scale: in a tumor-board registry the choice of TXR1i versus non-TXR1 systemic therapy follows prognosis (ECOG, prior lines, prior resistance, tumor burden, lineage, site, calendar period), so a crude risk difference is confounded. A conditional odds ratio from a regression is also not the requested quantity; the task asks for a marginal risk difference. Check: standardized mean differences of baseline covariates by therapy_class within the target population before and after adjustment (aim for |SMD|<0.1). Use IPTW, g-computation or AIPW standardised to the whole SV-positive target population, and report the marginal risk difference in percentage points with a bootstrap confidence interval.
briefing.reason: Determines the estimator for benefit_rd_pp; a crude or conditional estimate would not be the requested marginal effect.

briefing.text: Missing week-16 outcomes: the estimand is benefit 'as if all patients had an assessable week-16 visit' (a hypothetical estimand). A complete-case analysis of benefit16 among assessed16==1 is biased if assessability depends on arm, toxicity or prognosis. Check: model P(assessed16=1 | arm, baseline covariates) and compare assessment rates by arm, ECOG, tumor burden and tox_stop_8wk. If assessability is informative, estimate the counterfactual risks with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights combined with treatment weights, or with doubly robust AIPW/g-computation over all analysis-set cases in the target population. Do not count unassessed cases as failures. Report the complete-case estimate only as a sensitivity analysis.
briefing.reason: The task wording explicitly requires handling non-assessment; ignoring it or treating it as failure estimates a different quantity.

briefing.text: Post-treatment variable handling: tox_stop_8wk happens after treatment starts. Do not adjust for it in the propensity model or in the benefit outcome model, because that blocks part of the treatment effect. It may, however, be the main driver of a missing week-16 assessment. Check: cross-tabulate tox_stop_8wk by assessed16 within each arm. Keep the treatment model to baseline confounders only; if tox_stop is needed to explain missingness, let it enter only the censoring model (time-ordered IPCW or sequential g-formula). Run a sensitivity analysis without it and state the missing-at-random assumption being made.
briefing.reason: Prevents a specific modelling error (conditioning on a mediator) while still dealing with toxicity-driven missingness.

briefing.text: Toxicity estimand: the 8-week toxicity/discontinuation risk under TXR1i 'in the same target population' is a counterfactual risk for the whole target population, not the crude rate among those who happened to receive TXR1i. The crude rate is biased if treated cases differ from the whole target population in toxicity modifiers such as germline DLR1 metabolism, age or ECOG. Check: convert dlr1_hap1/dlr1_hap2 to an activity score by summing the per-allele activity values from dlr1_allele_table (CPIC convention), flag cases with low dlr1_call_confidence, and compare the activity-score distribution between treated cases and all target cases. Estimate the toxicity risk with g-computation or IPTW standardised to the whole SV-positive population, include the activity score as a covariate (with a sensitivity analysis for low-confidence calls), and keep all treated cases in the denominator.
briefing.reason: Determines the estimator for toxicity_dropout_risk_pp and flags a pharmacogenetic covariate the teams might otherwise overlook.

briefing.text: Positivity in a small subgroup: the SV-positive target population may be small, and some strata (site, calendar period, lineage) may have received only one therapy, giving extreme weights and unstable estimates. Check: propensity score overlap by arm, minimum and maximum weight, effective sample size per arm, and therapy by site and calendar_period within the target population. If overlap is poor, simplify the propensity model, use stabilised weights or AIPW rather than pure IPW, and report a weight-truncation sensitivity analysis. If a stratum has a structural zero, say so and state the narrowed population rather than extrapolating. One option to consider and justify is fitting nuisance models on a wider eligible cohort while standardising to the target population.
briefing.reason: Model complexity and estimator choice must be matched to the available sample, and the stability of the final sign of net utility depends on it.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team compared the toxicity rate of low-confidence DLR1 calls with that of high-confidence calls at the same activity-score value and found them to behave very differently, which made them doubt both the recorded score of those calls and the functional form of the activity-score term. Check whether that holds in your data: tabulate toxicity by activity-score level, split by call confidence. Does it change how the activity score and the low-confidence calls should enter your primary toxicity model, as opposed to a sensitivity analysis?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found a small effective sample size in the non-TXR1 systemic arm and a large maximum inverse-probability weight within the target population, and treated positivity as a real problem. You recorded positivity as not found, yet also recorded residual imbalance for one site and one period after weighting. Check the effective sample size per arm, the largest weights and which patients carry them in your target set. Does it change your method or how much you trust the benefit estimate?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team's target population has a slightly different number of cases from yours. They placed the ASE, phase-consistency, mapping-quality and breakpoint-homology cutoffs at different values, chosen from visible gaps in the distributions, used a fixed minimum split-molecule count rather than a depth-scaled one, and did not use read N50. They also estimated the treatment effect among the P2T cases their rule excluded, as a check that the rule separates true targets from the rest. List the cases that sit between plausible cutoffs in your data, check where the gaps in each distribution actually fall, and check the effect in the cases your rule excludes. Does it change your rule?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team describes the toxicity-stop variable as entering only the model for whether week 16 was assessed, not the outcome regression, and noted that the non-TXR1 systemic arm has very few toxicity-stop cases. Your outcome model conditions on toxicity stop. Check how many assessed patients each arm-by-toxicity-stop cell of your outcome model rests on, and whether your estimate still targets the marginal all-assessed effect once that post-treatment variable is in the outcome regression (is it averaged over its distribution under each arm?). Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team put the 8-week toxicity-stop variable in both the censoring model and the outcome regression of the sequential estimator, and then standardised over it, because among TXR1i patients who stopped for toxicity very few have an assessed week-16 outcome and the censoring weights for them are extreme, so the result for that group leans on the outcome model. Your notes say toxicity stop enters only the censoring model. Check in your data how many assessed patients there are in each arm-by-toxicity-stop cell, how extreme the censoring weights are, and whether your outcome regressions are consistent with the missingness assumption you make. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team's target population has a slightly different number of cases from yours. Their artifact cluster also used read N50 alongside segmental duplication, mapping quality, low complexity and homology, with somewhat different cutoffs; they required split-molecule support scaled to sequencing depth rather than a fixed count; and they placed the ASE and phase-consistency cutoffs at different values. They also saw that the estimate moves with the strength of ASE evidence inside the target set. Check whether read N50 and depth carry information about call quality in your data, which cases sit between plausible cutoffs, and whether your result is sensitive to those borderline cases. Does it change your rule?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team found that DLR1 activity score differs strongly between treatment arms and that, after weighting, imbalance remained for one site and one enrolment period. Check the weighted balance in your target set for each site, each period and the activity score, and check whether the activity score is in your propensity model for the benefit analysis as well as in the toxicity model. Does it change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: the other team noted that every low-confidence DLR1 call carries the same recorded activity-score value, and handled those calls with an indicator or by exclusion as sensitivity analyses, while you gave them their own level in the primary toxicity model. Check how the toxicity risk standardised to the whole target population moves across the ways of handling those calls (own level, excluded, recoded, taken at face value), and which of them matches what the data show about those calls. Does it change your primary choice?

referee.difference: Same estimator family (sequential doubly robust AIPW for the hypothetical benefit, AIPW TXR1i toxicity standardised to the target set). They differ in rows: X uses ASE>=0.65, phase>=0.70, MAPQ>=40, split>=3 (n=496, 146 SYS); Y uses ASE>=0.62, phase>=0.66, MAPQ>=42, split>=max(3,0.1*depth) (n=503, 153 SYS); 482 shared. Y's model form also yields a lower RD (22.2 vs 29.2).
referee.test: est.py: one common AIPW run on both sets to split the gap into rows vs modelling. border.py/altfrac.py/ccf.py: disputed cases and full admitted set compared on independent time-zero activation markers (alt_molecule_fraction, purity/copy-corrected junction copies per tumour cell, TXR1 TPM, local copy) with benefit by arm.
referee.expected_if_x: Y-only cases look non-target, X-only low-split cases look like core target cases, and the common estimator gives about 29 pp on X's set.
referee.expected_if_y: Y-only cases look like core target cases, X-only low-split cases look like artefacts, and Y's set gives about 22 pp.
referee.outcome: Common estimator: X set RD 29.3/tox 34.1/NU 17.4; Y set RD 25.8/tox 32.8/NU 14.4, so about half the gap is rows and half is Y's modelling. On the disputed rows X is right: X-only cases are core-like (alt fraction 0.16, ASE 0.81) and Y-only cases are not (alt fraction 0.04, lower TPM, TXR1i benefit 0.11). But both sets keep a shared cluster of 154 cases: alt_molecule_fraction is bimodal with a trough at 0.08-0.12, and this cluster has high local copy (median 5.4) and only about 0.27 junction copies per tumour cell versus about 0.9 in the main cluster. In this subclonal or amplification cluster TXR1i benefit is 3% vs 18% on SYS. Removing it gives RD 41.4, tox 33.5, NU 29.7 (on X rows RD 40.9, on Y rows RD 39.7).
referee.reason: Both teams admit a subclonal-junction, TXR1-amplified cluster that a time-zero marker separates cleanly. It is not SV-driven activation and dilutes the RD by about 12 pp. X is closer on the cases the teams dispute, but that is minor next to the shared error. Code 1 holds under every version. No bootstrap was run for own_answer (time limit).

own_answer.reasoning: Target: analysis_set=1, P2T, breakpoint QC (no segdup, MAPQ>=42, low complexity<0.4, homology<15bp), split>=3, junction<=100kb, ASE>=0.62, phase>=0.66, plus a clonal junction (alt_molecule_fraction>=0.08, at the bimodal trough), n=363 (260 TXR1i, 103 SYS). Benefit: sequential AIPW with baseline propensity; censoring and outcome models include week-8 toxicity, then standardised. Toxicity: AIPW risk under TXR1i with DLR1 activity categorical and low-confidence calls as their own level. NU = 41.4 - 0.35*33.51 = 29.67.
